# Settings Window Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The application's settings, which for now are the system prompts each tab of the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/ChatInputScope.md) sends.

### Shape

#### Description

Shown in an [InsetPanelScope](../../ui/components/inset-panel/InsetPanelScope.md) over the main window, not a window of its own. It is headed "Settings", with a close button whose tooltip says it closes the settings; closing the panel any way an inset panel closes closes them too. Beneath the heading, its page scrolls with a [ScrollbarScope](../../ui/components/scrollbar/ScrollbarScope.md).

#### Opening

It opens with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS) from anywhere in the application, or from whatever command opens the settings, in place of anything else in the inset panel. Opening it while it is already open leaves it as it is rather than opening another.

#### System Prompts

The page is headed "System prompts", with a muted line beneath saying that each tab gives a prompt sent from it this system prompt, that they are saved with the project as they are edited, and that the CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION placeholders stand for the code and spec locations and PITON_FLUENCY for the project's Piton fluency, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says.
Then, for each tab, in the order of the [PromptModesScope](../prompt-mode/modes/PromptModesScope.md): its name, the muted path of the file its prompt is saved in, and a "Reset to default" button, disabled while the prompt is already the default, which puts the default back and saves it. Beneath them, an editor for the prompt, 120 pixels tall before it scrolls, highlighting it as Piton, with soft wrapping and no line numbers or folding. A prompt that can't be read or saved says why beneath its editor.
Without a project open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/NoProjectStateScope.md) says, in place of the prompts it reads "Open a project to edit its system prompts."

#### Saving

The prompts belong to the project opened through the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/ProjectDirectoryScope.md), each saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/ProjectDataScope.md) says. Every edit is saved straight away. When the window loads the prompts, any tab with no file yet has its default saved, so every prompt can also be found and edited by hand. The prompts are read again each time the settings open and whenever another project is opened, so an edit made by hand shows up; a prompt that already shows what was read is left alone, so its cursor stays put.

#### Templates

A prompt is a template, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says, and a reset puts back its default.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../ui/theme/ThemeScope.md): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope

export scope ModeSystemPromptsScope:
    concept: {ModeSystemPromptsConcept}

concept ModeSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:
        The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of
        work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

    shape: {ModeSystemPromptsShape}

shape ModeSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        Each of the @{PromptModesScope} has a system prompt template. A prompt
        sent in a mode gives its hidden anchor a systemPrompt property,
        alongside its userPrompt, from that mode's template.

    templates:
        A template is Piton prose, like the prompt it is sent with, so it can
        reference the spec, with four placeholders, CODE_LOCATION,
        SPEC_LOCATION, PITON_FLUENCY, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE, each written
        after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation.
        Before the prompt is compiled, the first three are filled in:
        CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION with the code location and the spec
        location, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says, and PITON_FLUENCY with
        the project's Piton fluency. Each can be moved or removed, like any
        other text of the template.

        UNDERSTANDING_FILE stands for the path, from the project directory, of
        the task's understanding file, and is filled in as the prompt is sent,
        once the task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the
        queue is given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no
        understanding file, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing.

    pitonFluency:
        The Piton fluency is what `piton claude --print-prompt` prints, run in
        the project directory. It is run once, in the background, when the
        project is opened, and kept for as long as the project stays open, so
        every prompt sent meanwhile is given the same; a prompt sent before it
        has finished waits for it. Where `piton` isn't installed or fails,
        PITON_FLUENCY is filled in with nothing, and the prompt is sent without
        it. A template left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives
        no system prompt at all. What it prints is
        taken as text, never read as Piton: its braces, backslashes, and
        interpolations reach the harness exactly as printed.

    saving:
        Each project has its own templates, saved with its data, as the
        @{ProjectDataScope} says, a Markdown file per mode, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}. A mode with no file yet sends its default.

    understandingFile:
        Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short
        list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which
        the @{ReferencedSpecSidebarScope} shows as it changes. It is saved
        beside the task's history record, with the same name and the
        extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing
        else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the templates saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, one Markdown
        file per mode, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth
        for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built,
        so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing
        them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made
        without them.

        Every mode's default, Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask, says, after what the
        mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:

        "Links to .claude/reference/… in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one before changing anything it covers."

        Each then has PITON_FLUENCY, on a paragraph of its own. Ask's ends
        there. The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a
        paragraph of its own:

        \ Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the spec or reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](spec/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.pi)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another. \

        The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a
        template puts back. A project whose templates were saved before a
        default changed, such as before PITON_FLUENCY was added, keeps them as
        they are.

from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope

export scope ModeSystemPromptsScope:
    concept: {ModeSystemPromptsConcept}

concept ModeSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:
        The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of
        work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

    shape: {ModeSystemPromptsShape}

shape ModeSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        Each of the @{PromptModesScope} has a system prompt template. A prompt
        sent in a mode gives its hidden anchor a systemPrompt property,
        alongside its userPrompt, from that mode's template.

    templates:
        A template is Piton prose, like the prompt it is sent with, so it can
        reference the spec, with four placeholders, CODE_LOCATION,
        SPEC_LOCATION, PITON_FLUENCY, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE, each written
        after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation.
        Before the prompt is compiled, the first three are filled in:
        CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION with the code location and the spec
        location, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says, and PITON_FLUENCY with
        the project's Piton fluency. Each can be moved or removed, like any
        other text of the template.

        UNDERSTANDING_FILE stands for the path, from the project directory, of
        the task's understanding file, and is filled in as the prompt is sent,
        once the task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the
        queue is given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no
        understanding file, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing.

    pitonFluency:
        The Piton fluency is what `piton claude --print-prompt` prints, run in
        the project directory. It is run once, in the background, when the
        project is opened, and kept for as long as the project stays open, so
        every prompt sent meanwhile is given the same; a prompt sent before it
        has finished waits for it. Where `piton` isn't installed or fails,
        PITON_FLUENCY is filled in with nothing, and the prompt is sent without
        it. A template left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives
        no system prompt at all. What it prints is
        taken as text, never read as Piton: its braces, backslashes, and
        interpolations reach the harness exactly as printed.

    saving:
        Each project has its own templates, saved with its data, as the
        @{ProjectDataScope} says, a Markdown file per mode, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}. A mode with no file yet sends its default.

    understandingFile:
        Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short
        list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which
        the @{ReferencedSpecSidebarScope} shows as it changes. It is saved
        beside the task's history record, with the same name and the
        extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing
        else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the templates saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, one Markdown
        file per mode, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth
        for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built,
        so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing
        them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made
        without them.

        Every mode's default, Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask, says, after what the
        mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:

        "Links to .claude/reference/… in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one before changing anything it covers."

        Each then has PITON_FLUENCY, on a paragraph of its own. Ask's ends
        there. The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a
        paragraph of its own:

        \ Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the spec or reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](spec/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.pi)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another. \

        The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a
        template puts back. A project whose templates were saved before a
        default changed, such as before PITON_FLUENCY was added, keeps them as
        they are.

# Sidebar Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

A column along the left or right of the main window, holding panels one above the other, each a tool for the work beside it.

### Shape

#### Description

Every sidebar is a sidebar, as its own scope says: it names the side it runs along, how wide it starts and how narrow it can be dragged, and the panels it holds, and those decide how it is drawn. It runs along its side, with a thin line down the edge where it meets what it sits beside, and is resized by dragging that edge. It holds its panels one above the other, across its full width, with a single thin line between one panel and the next.

#### Sidebars

- left: the [ProjectSidebarScope](../project-sidebar/ProjectSidebarScope.md), along the left of the body, for finding your way around the project
- right: the [ReferencedSpecSidebarScope](../referenced-spec-sidebar/ReferencedSpecSidebarScope.md), at the right of the message list while a task runs

#### Panels

A panel is one tool in a sidebar, as its own scope says. What it is like follows from four things it names:

- its title: a panel with a title has a header reading it; one without has no header
- whether it is counted: a counted panel's header shows how many rows it lists, muted, at its right
- its height: a panel fills the height its sidebar's other panels leave, fits its contents, or shares the height left with the other panels that share it, by a line dragged between them
- whether it scrolls: one that scrolls has a [ScrollbarScope](../scrollbar/ScrollbarScope.md) of its own when its contents are taller than it

#### Headers

A panel's header is slightly contrasting to the panel's body: the header is on the theme's raised surface, a small step toward the viewer, and the body on its base surface, as the sidebar is, so the header reads as part of the panel, marked off from its body, with no line between them.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/ThemeScope.md): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

The spec and code are both updated. The spec builds with `piton build check`, all 245 tests pass, and clippy is clean on the files I touched. I haven't run the app to look at the new sidebar.

**Settings sidebar**
- A 180px column down the left lists two sections, "System prompts" and "Injected prompts". The picked one is highlighted with a thin accent bar on its left edge.

- "System prompts" works as before. "Injected prompts" holds the new spec-reading prompt, laid out the same way: its file path, a "Reset to default" button and an editor.

**Spec-reading prompt**
- It's saved per project as `.suspense/system-prompts/spec-reading.md`, and its default is built into the app like the other defaults. The default reads: *"Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/… in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one before changing anything it covers."*
- It goes into a template wherever `${SPEC_READING}` is written. Its own placeholders are filled in too.
- If it's left blank, its paragraph is dropped from the prompt, the same way a missing Piton fluency is.
- **This changes the defaults:** in all four mode defaults, `${SPEC_READING}` replaces the hard-coded "Links to .claude/reference/…" line.

- It's a constant in `src/harness.rs`. The app only runs `claude -p` today, so it is always `.claude`.
